volume_title: 29th International Conference on Theory and Applications of Satisfiability Testing (SAT 2026)
title: Long-Distance Q(D^std)-Consensus Is Sound
abstract: We describe a procedure that extracts existential strategies from verification proofs in the Long-Distance Consensus (i.e., Term Resolution) proof system when augmented with dependency schemes. We prove that when the standard dependency scheme 𝙳^std is used, the extracted strategies are winning strategies, thus establishing soundness of the proof system LDQ(D^std)-Consensus. We show through a counterexample that this approach fails to show soundness for LDQ(D^rrs)-Consensus.

      Abstract
We describe a procedure that extracts existential strategies from verification proofs in the Long-
Distance Consensus (i.e., Term Resolution) proof system when augmented with dependency schemes.
We prove that when the standard dependency scheme Dstd is used, the extracted strategies are
winning strategies, thus establishing soundness of the proof system LDQ(Dstd )-Consensus. We show
through a counterexample that this approach fails to show soundness for LDQ(Drrs )-Consensus.

/ Consensus, Dependency Schemes

 1      Introduction
Quantified Boolean formulas (QBFs) provide a succinct encoding for problems in PSPACE,
with significant applications in formal verification, synthesis, and planning [4, 9, 11, 17].
While SAT-based approaches remain the state of the art in many cases, QBF solver technology
has advanced rapidly through a variety of new techniques [13, 7, 14], supported by an evolving
theoretical understanding of underlying proof systems [3, 5, 6, 8].
    Modern search-based QBF solvers, such as those implementing the QCDCL algorithm [10,
19], generally operate by learning constraints to prune the search space. To establish the
falsity of a formula, solvers learn clauses via (long-distance) Q-resolution, whereas to establish
truth, they learn terms (or cubes) via (long-distance) Q-consensus. In both cases, the solver
is traditionally restricted by the variable dependencies induced by the quantifier prefix.
The solver DepQBF overcomes this in certain cases by using dependency schemes [13, 12],
which identify pairs of independent variables and allow the solver to bypass the prefix order,
significantly expanding the power of decision heuristics.
    The addition of dependency schemes to Q-resolution and Q-consensus has been shown to be
sound for Dstd and Drrs (the standard and reflexive resolution-path dependency schemes) [16],
and long-distance Q-resolution was shown to be sound for normal dependency schemes [15].
(Both Dstd and Drrs are normal schemes.) However, a significant gap remained on the dual
side of the calculus, as there was no proof of soundness for long-distance Q-consensus with
dependency schemes. The soundness proof for Q(D)-Consensus for D ∈ {Dstd , Drrs } shows
that countermodels with restricted dependencies are preserved by existential reduction [16],
but this does not work with syntactically contradictory cubes derived by LDQ-Consensus.
Moreover, while LDQ-Res derives clauses directly from the CNF matrix, LDQ-Consensus works
with cubes constructed on the fly from satisfying assignments. Since dependencies are defined

        2     Preliminaries

       2.1    Notation
       A literal is either a Boolean variable (a positive literal) or its negation (a negative literal).
       For a variable v, the polarity of a literal is pol(v) = 1 and pol(¬v) = 0. A clause C is a
       disjunction of literals; a cube or term T is a conjunction of literals. A formula in conjunctive
       normal form (CNF) is a conjunction of clauses. It is often convenient to view clauses
       and cubes as sets of literals, with the disjunction/conjunction implied by the context. A
       Quantified Boolean Formula Φ in prefix CNF form, referred to as PCNF QBF, consists of
       a prefix Q in which variables are quantified either existentially (∃x) or universally (∀y),
       followed by a CNF formula φ in these variables, called the matrix. We denote the QBF
       succinctly as Φ = Qφ.
           We denote by var(ℓ) the variable corresponding to a literal, and by var(φ) the set of
       variables appearing in a formula φ. (In particular, var(C) or var(T ) for a clause or cube
       is the set of variables appearing in it.) For a PCNF QBF Φ = Qφ, the set of existentially
       quantified variables is denoted var∃ (Φ) or E, and the set of universally quantified variables
       is denoted var∀ (Φ) or U . By var(Φ) we mean E ∪ U . For a variable v in Φ, qtype(v) is its
       quantifier type, in {∃, ∀}. We denote by L(v) and R(v) the variables (strictly) to the left and
       right of v in the quantifier prefix, respectively. Note that x ∈ L(v) if and only if v ∈ R(x),
       and we also denote this by x < v.
           For a set of variables S and a cube T , we denote by T |S the sub-cube obtained by
       discarding from T those literals ℓ with var(ℓ) ∈  / S.
           An assignment of a set of variables S is a function σ : S → {0, 1}. We say that σ satisfies
       a literal ℓ if σ(var(ℓ)) = pol(ℓ), and that σ satisfies a clause (or cube) if it satisfies at least
       one (respectively, every) literal in it.
           An existential strategy for Φ is an indexed family F = {fe }e∈E of Boolean functions,
       where each fe has assignments of the variables in L(e) as its domain. An assignment σ of
       E ∪ U is consistent with F if fe (σ|L(e) ) = σ(e) for each e ∈ E. The strategy F is winning
       (for existential) if every assignment consistent with F satisfies the matrix.
           By ITE(test, b1 , b2 ) we mean the branching rule “If the condition in test is satisfied,
       then pick value b1 , else pick value b2 .”
           A decision list computing a function f : {0, 1}m → {0, 1} is a sequence of rules of the
       form (fi , vi ), where each fi is a Boolean function, each vi is in {0, 1}, and the final rule has
       a function that is always true. On an assignment σ, the value computed by the list is vi ,

    Given a PCNF QBF Qφ, the universal reduction of a clause C is the reduced clause
C \ {ℓ ∈ C | var(ℓ) ∈ var∀ (Φ); for all ℓ′ ∈ C with var(ℓ′ ) ∈ var∃ (Φ), var(ℓ′ ) < var(ℓ)}.

2.2    Dependency Schemes
A dependency scheme D maps each PCNF formula Φ to a subset of the pairs of variables in
(E × U ) ∪ (U × E).

▶ Definition 1 (Trivial Dependency Scheme). The trivial dependency scheme Dtrv maps each
PCNF formula Φ to the relation

   Dtrv
    Φ = {(x, y) ∈ var(Φ) × var(Φ) | x < y, qtype(x) ̸= qtype(y)}.

▶ Definition 2 (X-Path). Let X ⊆ var(Φ). An X-path in φ is a sequence C1 , . . . , Cr
of clauses from φ such that consecutive clauses share variables in X; that is, var(Ci ) ∩
var(Ci+1 ) ∩ X ̸= ∅ for 1 ≤ i < r. We say that variables x and y are connected with respect
to X if there is an X-path C1 , . . . , Cr such that x ∈ var(C1 ) and y ∈ var(Cr ).

▶ Definition 3 (Standard Dependency Scheme). The standard dependency scheme Dstd maps
each PCNF formula Φ to the relation

   Dstd            trv
    Φ = {(x, y) ∈ DΦ | x and y are connected with respect to R(x) ∩ var∃ (Φ)}.

The reflexive resolution-path dependency scheme Drrs is defined as follows [16].

▶ Definition 4 (Resolution Path). Let X ⊆ var∃ (Φ). A resolution path in Φ via X is a
sequence ℓ1 , . . . , ℓ2k of literals satisfying the following properties:
1. For all i ∈ [k], there is a clause Ci ∈ φ such that ℓ2i−1 , ℓ2i ∈ Ci .
2. For all i ∈ [k], var(ℓ2i−1 ) ̸= var(ℓ2i ).
3. For all i ∈ [k − 1], var(ℓ2i ) ∈ X.
4. For all i ∈ [k − 1], ¬ℓ2i = ℓ2i+1 .
We say that ℓ1 and ℓ2k are connected by resolution in Φ with respect to X.

▶ Definition 5 (Dependency Pair). Let x, y ∈ var(Φ). We say {x, y} is a dependency pair of
Φ with respect to X ⊆ var∃ (Φ) if at least one of the following conditions holds:
   x and y, as well as ¬x and ¬y, are connected by resolution with respect to X.
   x and ¬y, as well as ¬x and y, are connected by resolution with respect to X.

▶ Definition 6 (Reflexive Resolution-Path Dependency Scheme). The reflexive resolution-path
dependency scheme Drrs maps each PCNF formula Φ = Qφ to the relation

   Drrs            trv
    Φ = {(x, y) ∈ DΦ | {x, y} is a dependency pair of Φ w.r.t. R(x) ∩ var∃ (Φ)}.


2.3    Consensus Proofs
A cube T is said to be a hitting cube or initial cube for Φ if it contains at least one literal
from every clause of φ.
   Consensus (cube resolution) on the cubes T1 ∪ {u} and T2 ∪ {¬u} results in the cube
T = T1 ∪ T2 . Here u is referred to as the pivot.

            For a dependency scheme D, existential reduction (with respect to D) of a variable e ∈ E
       from a cube T removes all literals of e from T , provided no literal of universal variable u
       with (e, u) ∈ DΦ appears in T . Since this paper deals exclusively with cube derivations, we
       often abbreviate this to reduction and omit D when it is clear from context.
            A Q(D)-Consensus proof, or verification, of Φ is a sequence of non-contradictory cubes
       T1 , T2 , . . . , Tk where Tk = ∅, and for each i ∈ [k], Ti is either an initial cube for Φ, or is
       obtained from Tj for some j < i by existential reduction, or is obtained from Tj and Tj ′ for
       some j, j ′ < i by consensus.
            Long-distance consensus allows derived cubes that contain literals e, ¬e for an existential
       variable e; the literals are considered to be merged, sometimes denoted e∗ . This is allowed
       if u < e holds, where u is the pivot. This can be generalized with a dependency scheme D
       by requiring (e, u) ∈    / DΦ . More precisely, long-distance D-consensus can be applied on the
       cubes T1 ∪ {u} and T2 ∪ {¬u} resulting in the cube T = T1 ∪ T2 provided that, for each
       e ∈ var∃ (Φ) with e ∈ T1 and ¬e ∈ T2 , or ¬e ∈ T1 and e ∈ T2 , (e, u) ∈   / DΦ .
            An LDQ(D)-Consensus verification of Φ is a sequence of cubes ending with the empty
       cube, where each cube is either an initial cube, or is obtained from earlier cubes through
       either existential reduction or through long-distance D-consensus.
            The Q-Consensus proof system – essentially Q(D)-Consensus with D = Dtrv – was first
       introduced in [1]. In [16], non-trivial dependency schemes were added and the Q(D)-Consensus
       proof system was first defined. In these papers, as well as in much of the subsequent literature,
       the system is called Q(D)-term resolution. However, Consensus has also been used in the
       literature for term-resolution, and we use that nomenclature here. The Long-Distance
       Resolution proof system was considered in [18, 1], and was extended with the use dependency
       schemes to LDQ(D)-Res in [15]. The LDQ(D)-Consensus proof systems defined above are the
       direct consensus analogues of the LDQ(D)-Res proof systems.


        3      Q-Consensus with Standard Dependencies

       Let Φ = Qφ be a PCNF formula. Without loss of generality, we assume that each clause
       in φ is universally reduced (using ordinary universal reduction, not the dependency-aware
       version). Let P = T1 , . . . , Tk be a Q(Dstd )-Consensus proof. Without loss of generality, we
       will assume that existential reduction is applied as early as possible and starting with the
       rightmost variable.


       3.1     Strategy Extraction for Q-Consensus with Standard Dependencies
       For each existential variable e, define the set

            D(e) = {e} ∪ {x ∈ L(e) | x and e are connected with respect to R(x) ∩ var∃ (Φ)}.

       That is, D(e) is the set of variables e depends on, according to the standard dependency
       scheme, including existential variables whose dependencies are included in those of variable e.

       ▶ Lemma 7. Let e and y be existential variables such that y ∈ D(e). Then D(y) ⊆ D(e).

       Proof. For e = y the statement is trivial. Now consider y ̸= e. Since y ∈ D(e), y and e are
       connected with respect to R(y) ∩ var∃ (Φ). For any x ∈ D(y), x and y are connected with
       respect to R(x) ∩ var∃ (Φ). Because R(y) ⊆ R(x), we can compose the corresponding paths to
       conclude that x and e are connected with respect to R(x) ∩ var∃ (Φ), proving x ∈ D(e). ◀

We extract decision lists representing an existential strategy from P with a slightly modified
version of the approach of Balabanov and Jiang [1]. Their strategy extraction algorithm
considers existential reduction steps in their order of appearance in the proof. For an
existential reduction step that derives Ti from Tj = Ti ∧ ℓ (where j < i), a rule (Ti , pol(ℓ)) is
added to the decision list of var(ℓ). Our only modification is that we restrict the condition
Ti to D(e) and add a rule (Ti |D(e) , pol(ℓ)), where e = var(ℓ). Since D(e) \ {e} ⊆ L(e), the

decision list:

    (Ti1 |D(e) , pol(ℓ1 )), (Ti2 |D(e) , pol(ℓ2 )), (Ti3 |D(e) , pol(ℓ3 )), . . . , (Tip |D(e) , pol(ℓp )), (⊤, 1).

▶ Lemma 9. Let σ : var(Φ) → {0, 1} be an assignment that is consistent with the extracted
strategy from Definition 8. For each existential variable e, there is an initial cube T such
that σ satisfies T |D(e) .

Using Lemma 9, we can prove that the strategy is winning for existential.

▶ Theorem 10. Let T1 , T2 , . . . , Tk be a Q(Dstd )-Consensus proof of Φ = Qφ. Any assignment
σ : var(Φ) → {0, 1} consistent with the strategy extracted as per Definition 8 satisfies the
matrix φ.

Proof. (Assuming Lemma 9) Let C ∈ φ be an arbitrary clause in the matrix. We have to
show that σ satisfies C. Let e ∈ var(C) be the rightmost existential variable in C. Since

is satisfied by σ. Since T is a hitting set for the clauses, it must contain a literal ℓ ∈ C, and
var(ℓ) ∈ D(e) by choice of e. So ℓ ∈ T |D(e) , and σ satisfies C.                               ◀

    4    Long-Distance Q-Consensus with Standard Dependencies
We generalize the strategy extraction algorithm for LDQ-Consensus by Balabanov, Jiang,
Janota, and Widl [2]. This involves associating each occurrence of contradictory literals e, ¬e
in a cube T with a phase function ψ(e), and replacing existential literals in cubes with their
phase functions to obtain shadow cubes which are then used in the decision lists.

4.1      Definition of Phase Functions, Shadow Cubes, and the Strategy
The phase function is either undefined or a Boolean circuit that determines which of the two
literals e and ¬e would end up in the cube under a restriction of the proof by an assignment
of the universal pivot variables.
▶ Definition 11. Let T1 , . . . , Tk be an LDQ(Dstd )-Consensus proof of a PCNF formula Φ. Let
e be an existential variable.
1. For an initial cube Ti , the phase function ψi (e) is defined as ψi (e) := ⊤ if e ∈ Ti ,
    ψi (e) := ⊥ if ¬e ∈ Ti , and ψi (e) := undef otherwise. This is well defined since initial
   cubes are non-contradictory.
2. If Tj is derived from Ti by reduction of variable e, then ψj (e) := undef, and ψj (y) := ψi (y)
    for y ∈ E \ {e}.
3. If Tr is derived from Ti ⊇ {u} and Tj ⊇ {¬u} by consensus on pivot variable u, we
   distinguish three cases:
   a. If one of ψi (e) and ψj (e) is undefined (i.e., if there is no merge), we set ψr (e) to the
       other (possibly also undefined) phase function.

       Before turning to the formal argument, we sketch the intuition behind the construction in

       in the two antecedents. The definition does this in one of two ways: either by combining
       them with an ITE guarded by u (case 3(c), used when (u, e) ∈ Dstd    Φ ), or by taking the phase
       function from one of the antecedents (case 3(b), used when (u, e) ∈    / Dstd
                                                                                 Φ ). With dependency
       schemes, one might worry that both cases apply in the same consensus step. Consider a step
       on pivot u that merges variables e1 and e2 with e1 < u < e2 , (e1 , u) ∈ / Dstd                 std

       the phase function of e1 is taken directly from one antecedent, while that of e2 is built with
       an ITE. It is not clear this yields a consistent strategy.

       D(e) for a single existential e. If e1 , e2 ∈ D(e), then e1 is connected to e with respect to
       R(e1 ) ∩ var∃ (Φ), e is connected to e2 with respect to R(e2 ) ∩ var∃ (Φ) ⊆ R(e1 ) ∩ var∃ (Φ), and
       u is connected to e2 with respect to R(u) ∩ var∃ (Φ) ⊆ R(e1 ) ∩ var∃ (Φ) (using e1 < u < e2 ).

       merged. So within D(e) all merged variables fall under the same case, and picking the phase
       function from a fixed side gives a consistent strategy.

▶ Theorem 14. The proof system LDQ(Dstd )-Consensus is sound.
Proof. The proof is identical to that of Theorem 10, except that we use Lemma 13 instead
of Lemma 9. It thus establishes that the strategy extracted from an LDQ(Dstd )-Consensus
proof using shadow cubes and phase functions is a winning strategy for existential. This
implies that the QBF is true, and so the proof system LDQ(Dstd )-Consensus is sound.   ◀

         5        Conclusion
        We have shown that LDQ(Dstd )-Consensus is a sound proof system for true QBFs, by giving
        a linear-time strategy extraction algorithm. Prior to this work, no polynomial-time strategy
        extraction was known even for the weaker system Q(Dstd )-Consensus (soundness there was
        established only indirectly, via preservation of countermodels [16]). Our result has a direct
        practical implication for solvers such as DepQBF [14]: long-distance resolution can now be
        combined with the standard dependency scheme and a winning strategy for the existential
        player can be extracted efficiently from the resulting proof when the QBF is true. Whether
        LDQ(Drrs )-Consensus is sound remains open. As shown in Section 3.2, our strategy extraction
        already fails for Q(Drrs )-Consensus, so settling this will require a different technique.
